Some experience: 20-second explainers, more time on practice
Regular user: 10-second recaps, straight to practice

exercise.task: Get a photosynthesis worksheet your Class 7 can actually do.
exercise.head: Worksheet: Photosynthesis

chips.t: Please make it really good.
chips.note: “Make it good” gave the AI nothing to work with.

chips.t: It is for Class 7, mixed reading levels.
chips.no: 1. Describe the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane.
chips.yes: 1. What three things does a plant need to make food?

chips.t: Give 5 questions with an answer key.
chips.no: … and 23 more questions, with no answers
chips.yes: … 4 more questions, with an answer key

chips.t: IMPORTANT!!! EASY!!!
Use short sentences and everyday words.
chips.no: Instructions: Attempt all questions with reference to the prescribed text.
chips.yes: Instructions: Write short answers. One line is enough.

exercise.head: Lesson plan: Fractions

chips.t: It is Class 5's first lesson on fractions.
chips.no: Start: Revise equivalent fractions from last year.
chips.yes: Start: Fold a paper in half. “This is one half.”

chips.t: Make it the best lesson plan ever.
chips.note: “Best ever” told the AI nothing new.

chips.t: I have one 40-minute period.
chips.no: Length: a 3-day unit with an assessment.

chips.t: I have only chalk, a board and paper.
chips.no: Activity: a tablet quiz and a projector slideshow.
chips.yes: Activity: pair work with paper strips and chalk.

chips.t: Think step by step.
chips.note: It sounded clever and changed nothing here.

exercise.task: Write a note asking parents to help with reading practice at home.
exercise.base: Write a message to parents about reading.
exercise.head: Message to parents

chips.t: Make it professional.
Parents are busy and will read it on a phone.
chips.no: Dear Parent/Guardian, it has been observed that reading proficiency is below the expected standard.
chips.yes: Namaste! A short note about reading this term.

chips.t: Be warm and respectful, not complaining.
chips.no: Parents have not been monitoring reading at home.
chips.yes: Your child is working hard, and a little help at home goes a long way.

chips.t: Use impressive words.
chips.note: Impressive words are harder to read.

chips.t: End with one request: 10 minutes of reading a day.
chips.yes: Could you listen to them read aloud for 10 minutes each evening?

exercise.task: Get an explanation of day and night that a Class 4 child will follow.
exercise.head: Why we have day and night

chips.t: It is for a 9-year-old in Class 4.
chips.no: The Earth rotates on an axis inclined at 23.5° to its orbital plane.
chips.yes: The Earth is like a ball that keeps turning.

chips.t: Use an example from daily life.
chips.no: The terminator line divides the illuminated hemisphere from the dark one.
chips.yes: Shine a torch on a ball: the bright side is day, the dark side is night.
chips.good: Uses a torch and a ball

chips.t: Explain it properly.
Be very detailed.
chips.note: “Very detailed” made it longer, not clearer.

chips.t: Keep it to 4 short sentences.
chips.bad: Too long to use in class

concepts.title: Why the first worksheet never fits
concepts.q: I don't understand what I am supposed to add.

concepts.title: Tell the AI who your students are
concepts.q: The questions are too hard for my class.

check.stem: You ask for a worksheet on the water cycle. The questions come back far too hard for your Class 4. What do you add to the prompt?

options.t: PLEASE MAKE IT EASY!!!
options.why: Easy for whom? Capital letters tell the AI nothing new.

options.t: It is for Class 4, and this is their first time with the topic.
options.why: One line about the students moves the level of every question.

options.t: Make it the best worksheet possible.
options.why: “Best” does not tell the AI who it is writing for.

concepts.title: Say how much you want
concepts.q: There are far too many questions, and no answers.

check.stem: The AI returns 28 questions and no answers. You have one period. What do you add?

options.t: Give six questions with an answer key.
options.why: A number, and the key in the same prompt. The AI stops guessing.

options.t: Keep it short.
options.why: Short compared to what? The AI still has to guess. Give a number.

options.t: Do not give too many questions.
options.why: How many is too many? Give a number.

concepts.title: Ask for simple words
concepts.q: The language is too difficult for my students.

check.stem: Your students know the science but trip on the wording of the questions. What do you add?

options.t: Use professional language.
options.why: “Professional” makes it longer and stiffer.

options.t: Explain every question in detail.
options.why: That gives them more words to trip on.

options.t: Use short sentences and everyday words.
options.why: Say how the language should sound and the AI rewrites everything that way.

concepts.title: Check it before you print
concepts.q: Can I trust the answer key?

check.stem: The worksheet looks right. What do you do before printing 40 copies?

options.t: Print it. The AI is usually right.
options.why: AI makes mistakes with facts, and it makes them with full confidence.

options.t: Read the answer key and solve the worksheet once yourself.
options.why: The AI drafts. The check has to be yours.

options.t: Ask the AI if it is sure.
options.why: It will say yes. The check has to be yours.

concepts.title: A lesson plan in 30 seconds
concepts.q: I don't understand what I am supposed to add.

concepts.title: Say the class and what they already know
concepts.q: The plan is too advanced for my students.

check.stem: The plan opens with “revise last year's decimals”. Your class has never met decimals. What do you add?

options.t: It is Class 5's first lesson on decimals.
options.why: The class gives the age. “First lesson” gives the starting point. You need both.

options.t: Make it the best lesson plan ever.
options.why: “Best ever” tells the AI nothing new.

options.t: Add more revision.
options.why: There is nothing to revise yet. Say where the class really is.

concepts.title: Give it your time limit
concepts.q: The plan is far too long for one period.

check.stem: The plan is a five-day unit. You have one period tomorrow. What do you add?

options.t: Make it shorter.
options.why: Shorter than what? Give the minutes.

options.t: Remove the homework.
options.why: That trims one item. The plan still does not fit a period.

options.t: I have one 40-minute period. Put the minutes next to each step.
options.why: With an exact limit, the AI cuts the plan to fit the bell.

concepts.title: Tell it what is in your room
concepts.q: It asks for things my school doesn't have.

check.stem: The activity needs a projector and tablets. Your room has a blackboard. What do you add?

options.t: Use modern teaching methods.
options.why: That invites even more gadgets.

options.t: I have only chalk, a board and paper, and 45 students.
options.why: List what you really have and the activities change to match.

options.t: Make the activity fun.
options.why: Fun, but still on tablets. Say what you have.

concepts.title: Messages parents will read
concepts.q: I don't understand what I am supposed to add.

concepts.title: Say who is reading, and where
concepts.q: It sounds like an office circular.

check.stem: The draft is a long formal letter. Most parents will see it on WhatsApp. What do you add?

options.t: Make it professional.
options.why: “Professional” makes it stiffer and longer.

options.t: Parents are busy and will read it on a phone. Keep it to four lines.
options.why: Tell the AI who is reading and on what.

options.t: Add a proper subject line and a reference number.
options.why: That makes it even more of a circular.

concepts.title: Name the tone
concepts.q: The tone feels like I am blaming the parents.

check.stem: One line in the draft says “parents are not checking homework”. What do you add?

options.t: Be strict, so parents take it seriously.
options.why: A parent who feels blamed gets defensive, or scolds the child.

options.t: Use impressive words.
options.why: Harder to read, and the blame is still there.

options.t: Be warm and respectful, not complaining.
options.why: Say the tone in plain words and the AI follows it closely.

concepts.title: End with one ask
concepts.q: Parents won't know what to do after reading it.

check.stem: The message ends “kindly take necessary action”. What do you add?

options.t: End with one request: sign the diary every Friday.
options.why: One small, clear step that a parent can do.

options.t: End politely.
options.why: Polite, but the parent still does not know what to do.

options.t: List everything parents should do this term.
options.why: Ask for five things and none of them get done.

classes.title: Worksheets that fit your class
classes.cut_by: Claude, in the build session, from the prompt in cut_prompt.txt (the API path was not run: no key)
sentences: Hello, teachers!
Today we make a worksheet with AI.
Ask an AI for a worksheet and you get one in seconds, but it does not know your class, so it writes for nobody in particular.
Last year, I asked for a worksheet on photosynthesis for my class 7.
I got 24 questions.
The first one asked about light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane.
That is a college question.
My students would have closed the notebook at question one.
The AI was not wrong.
It just did not know who it was writing for.
The fix is simple.
Tell the AI three things, who your students are, how much you want, and how simple the words should be.
Same AI, same topic, and now the worksheet fits your classroom.
In this class, we take them one at a time, with the same photosynthesis worksheet. At the end, we check the worksheet before it goes to print.
Rule 1. Tell the AI who your students are.
Say the class and the level, and the questions come down to match.
The AI cannot see your classroom.
It does not know if you teach class 3 or a teacher training college. When it does not know, it aims at the middle of everything it has read, and most of that was written for adults.
One line about your students changes its target.
Let us try it.
Here is the first prompt.
Make a worksheet on photosynthesis.
And here is question one from the AI.
Describe the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane.
Too hard for Class 7.
Now I add one line to the prompt.
It is for Class 7 with mixed reading levels.
I send it again.
Look at question one now.
What three things does a plant need to make food?
That is a question my class 7 can answer.
Sunlight, water and air.
I did not ask the AI to be easy.
I did not write the word simple.
I only said who the students are, and the level changed by itself. If your class has children who read slowly,
say that too.
Mixed reading levels is a useful phrase.
The AI will then mix easy and medium questions.
A common mistake here is to shout.
Teachers type, IMPORTANT, MAKE IT EASY, in capital letters.
Capital letters tell the AI nothing new.
Easy for whom?
Easy for a class 10 student is hard for class 5.
Give the class, not the adjective.
Rule 2. Say how much you want.
Ask for a number of questions and ask for the answer key.
If you do not give a number, the AI guesses, and it likes to be generous.
It will give you 20 or 30 questions, because more looks more helpful. But you have one period of 40 minutes, and you have to correct every notebook.
Back to our worksheet.
The level is right now, but look at the length.
24 questions and no answers. So I add one more line to the prompt.
Give five questions with an answer key.
I send it.
Now there are five questions and under them.
5 answers.
That fits one period, and the correction takes me 10 minutes instead of an hour. You can go one step further.
Tell it the kinds of questions.
For example, two fill in the blanks, two one-line answers, and one diagram to label.
The AI follows that list exactly.
I often ask for the marks too.
Five questions, ten marks in total.
Then the worksheet is ready to become a small class test.
One more tip.
Always ask for the answer key in the same prompt.
If you ask later, the AI sometimes changes the questions.
Ask once, and you get the questions and the answers together.
Rule 3. Ask for simple words.
Tell the AI how the language should sound. Short sentences and everyday words.
The AI learned to write from textbooks, reports, and websites.
So its natural voice sounds like a textbook. For many of our students,
English is a second or third language.
A child may know the science and still get stuck on the wording of the question.
Look at the instruction line on our worksheet.
It says, "Attempt all questions with reference to the prescribed text."
No 12 year old talks like that.
So I add the third line to the prompt.
Use short sentences and everyday words.
I send it.
The instruction now says...
Write short answers.
One line is enough. And the questions changed as well. Before, it asked,
What is the significance of chlorophyll?
Now it asks.
What does the green color in a leaf do?
Same idea in words a child uses.
You can also name the language level.
I sometimes write.
Use English that a Class 5 student can read. Or ask for the worksheet in Telugu or Hindi, if that is the language of your classroom.
Do not ask for impressive language.
Do not ask it to be professional.
Those words make the worksheet longer and stiffer.
Ask for the opposite.
Short, plain and clear.
Before you print,
check the worksheet yourself. The AI drafts.
You are the teacher.
Here is the full prompt we built.
Make a worksheet on photosynthesis.
It is for Class 7 with mixed reading levels.
Give five questions with an answer key.
Use short sentences and everyday words.
Four short lines.
It took me under a minute to type.
Now the checking.
First, I read the answer key.
AI makes mistakes with facts, and it makes them with full confidence. In one of my worksheets, the key said plants breathe in oxygen to make food.
That is wrong.
It is carbon dioxide.
If I had printed it, 40 children would have learned it wrong.
Second, I check against my textbook.
The AI does not know which chapter we finished.
If question 4 is from next month's lesson, I remove it.
Third, I solve the worksheet once as a student.
If I need more than 15 minutes, it is too long for my class.
If something is wrong, you do not start again.
Just tell the AI what to change.
Question 3 is too hard, make it simpler. Or, replace question 4 with one about sunlight.
It keeps the rest and fixes that one part.
Let us close.
Three things to tell the AI every time. Who your students are.
How much you want, how simple the words should be, and one thing for you to do.
Check before you print.
Try it today with the next topic in your own syllabus.
Your first prompt will take two minutes. By the end of the week, it will take 30 seconds. In the next class, we use the same idea to plan a whole lesson.

classes.title: A lesson plan you can teach tomorrow
classes.cut_by: Claude, in the build session, from the prompt in cut_prompt.txt (the API path was not run: no key)
sentences: Hello again, teachers.
A good lesson plan takes about an hour to write.
An AI can draft one in 30 seconds, but the draft is only as good as what you tell it.
Ask for a lesson plan on fractions and you may get a three-day unit with a projector, tablets and revision of things your class never learned.
So give it three things, the class and what they already know, the time you have and what is in your room.
Then you fix the draft because you are the teacher.
Today's example is the first lesson on fractions for Class 5.
First, say the class and what they already know. Then the plan starts in the right place.
The AI cannot tell what your students have learned.
If you only say fractions, it may assume they met fractions last year.
It will start with revision of something that was never taught.
Here is my first prompt.
Write a lesson plan on fractions.
The plan begins like this.
Start: revise equivalent fractions from last year.
My class 5 has never seen a fraction, so I add one line.
It is Class 5's first lesson on fractions.
Now the plan begins.
Fold a paper in half.
This is one half.
That is where a first lesson should begin, with something the children can hold.
Notice the two parts of that line.
Class 5 tells it the age.
First lesson tells it the starting point.
You need both.
If your class is behind, say so.
For example, most of them still find division hard.
The plan will slow down and add practice.
A common mistake is to write.
Make it the best lesson plan ever!
Best ever tells the AI nothing new.
It was already trying its best.
Tell it about the children instead.
Second, give it your time limit.
Tell the AI exactly how long you have.
And it cuts the plan to fit the bell.
Without a time limit,
The AI plans for an ideal school with no bell.
You get an introduction, three activities, group work, a quiz and homework review.
On paper it is lovely.
In a real period, you would finish a third of it.
Look at our fractions plan.
At the top it says, length: a three-day unit with an assessment.
I have one period.
So I add, I have one 40-minute period.
I send it again.
Now it says, length: one 40-minute period, in four steps.
Five minutes to start, 15 to teach,
15 to practice, 5 to close.
Every step has its minutes written next to it.
That is a plan I can follow with a clock on the wall.
If you lose time to attendance, tell it that too.
I write.
The first five minutes go to attendance.
It then plans for 35 minutes, which is the truth.
Ask for the minutes next to every step. Then, when the class runs late, you can see at a glance which step to drop.
Third, tell it what is in your room.
List what you really have and the activities change to match.
The AI has read thousands of lesson plans from schools with smart boards and one tablet for each child.
So that is what it suggests.
It is not showing off.
It simply does not know your room.
In our plan, the activity says, a tablet quiz and a projector slideshow.
My school has neither, so I add the third line.
I have only chalk, a board, and paper.
Now, the activity is pair work with paper strips and chalk.
Each pair folds a strip into halves, then quarters and writes the fraction on it.
That costs nothing and I can do it tomorrow morning. You can list other things as well.
45 students in the room.
Benches that do not move.
No printer.
Each of these changes the plan. With fixed benches, it stops asking for circles and group corners. With no printer, it stops asking for handouts.
Do not be shy about what your school lacks. The AI is not judging. The more honest the list, the more usable the plan.
So,
Three lines for every lesson plan. The class and what they know. The time you have.
What is in your room.
Our full prompt was, write a lesson plan on fractions.
It is Class 5's first lesson on fractions.
I have one 40-minute period.
I have only chalk, a board, and paper.
Read the draft once.
Change what does not suit your children and it is ready.
The AI drafts. You decide.

classes.title: Messages parents will read
classes.cut_by: Claude, in the build session, from the prompt in cut_prompt.txt (the API path was not run: no key)
sentences: Hello, teachers!
Today, messages to parents.
A note to parents has to be short, kind, and clear.
An AI can draft one in seconds, but it guesses the tone, and it usually guesses wrong.
Ask for a message about reading and you get an office circular.
Dear parent or guardian, it has been observed and so on.
Parents stop reading at the second line.
So tell it three things.
Who is reading, the tone you want, and the one thing parents should do. Then read it once as a parent before you send it.
Our example today is a note asking parents to help with reading practice at home.
First, say who is reading and where.
A parent on a phone needs four lines, not a circular.
The AI does not know your parents.
It does not know that most of them will open this on WhatsApp, on a small screen, on the bus home from work. When it does not know,
it writes a formal letter, because school letters on the internet look like that.
Here is the first prompt.
Write a message to parents about reading.
The draft begins.
Dear parent or guardian.
It has been observed that reading proficiency is below the expected standard.
Now I add one line.
Parents are busy and will read it on a phone.
I send it again.
The new message begins, Namaste!
A short note about reading this term.
It is four lines long.
No paragraphs to scroll through.
You can tell it more about the readers.
Many parents in my school
read Telugu more easily than English.
So I add, write it in simple Telugu.
Some parents ask a neighbor to read messages to them.
Then I ask for very short sentences, which are easy to read aloud.
Do not write, make it professional. Professional makes it stiffer and longer. For a parent, professional means clear and respectful, and you can ask for exactly that.
Second, name the tone.
Say it in plain words.
Warm, respectful, not complaining.
The AI follows it closely.
Tone is where AI drafts go wrong most often. When the subject is a problem, like weak reading,
the AI writes like a complaint. And a parent who feels blamed does not help.
They get defensive or they scold the child.
In our draft, one line says, "Parents have not been monitoring reading at home."
Imagine receiving that after a 12-hour shift.
So I add, be warm and respectful, not complaining.
The line becomes, "Your child is working hard and a little help at home goes a long way."
Same message.
The child needs to read at home.
But now the parent is on our side.
Here is a trick I use.
I describe the tone as a person.
Write like a kind class teacher talking to a parent at the school gate.
The AI understands a person better than a list of adjectives.
After the AI writes it,
Read the message aloud once.
If you would not say a sentence to a parent's face, remove it.
Third, end with one ask.
Decide the one thing you want parents to do and ask the AI to end with exactly that.
Most school messages end with "kindly take necessary action."
What action?
The parent does not know, so nothing happens.
A message works when the parent knows the next step, and the step is small.
Our draft ends that way. Kindly take necessary action. So I add the last line.
End with one request.
10 minutes of reading a day.
Now it ends.
Could you listen to them read aloud for 10 minutes each evening?
That is something a parent can do tonight.
Even a parent who cannot read English can listen and encourage.
Keep it to one request.
If you ask for reading and homework checks and a meeting and the fee, parents do none of them.
One message, one ask.
If you need a reply, say how.
For example, reply yes on WhatsApp. Then you can count who has seen it.
And give a time.
10 minutes each evening is clear. Regularly is not.
That is the whole method.
Who is reading.
The tone.
One ask.
Our full prompt was, "Write a message to parents about reading."
Parents are busy and will read it on a phone.
Be warm and respectful, not complaining.
End with one request.
Ten minutes of reading a day. Before you press send, read it once as a parent.
If it sounds like a friend who cares about your child,
send it.
